eyebrow: ACM CAIS 2026 · San Jose, California · May 26 to 29, 2026
headline: What CAIS 2026 built, and what it chose to recognize
standfirst: Sixty papers converged on one project this year: composing AI systems out of many interacting parts. Most of the work was construction. The work the field named outstanding was the work that made those systems trustworthy.

numbers.label: CAIS 2026, by the record
numbers.caption: Final figures, June 2026. Registration reached capacity.

composition.heading: The program
composition.summary: Sixty peer-reviewed papers ran across these five tracks, selected from 170 reviewed submissions. Alongside them: 46 system demonstrations (45 in the archival proceedings), 3 operational-experience talks, 5 workshops, and 1 tutorial.

orientationSeam: This recap groups the year's 60 papers into three movements, matching what the field spent 2026 doing: building agentic systems (Build), measuring whether they work (Measure), and making them safe to trust (Secure). Each movement features a few standout papers, and the full winners list is at the end.

movements.label: Build
movements.headline: Most of the year’s work was construction: assembling agents, models, and tools into systems that hold.
movements.framing: Thirty-seven of the sixty papers, more than three in five, take up architecture and composition, plus the optimization and operations that make composed systems run. The volume is itself the finding. In 2026 the field’s main occupation was not a better single model but the discipline of putting many parts together into something dependable.

featured.title: optimize_anything: Unified Text Optimization can Outperform Specialized Systems
featured.authors: Lakshya A Agrawal, Donghyun Lee, et al.
featured.gloss: Opens the proceedings and is the only contribution recognized in both the paper and demo tracks: one text-optimization method that matches or beats systems hand-built for a specific task.

featured.title: The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate
featured.gloss: A result about composing well rather than composing more: for these tasks, agents correcting themselves in isolation outperform an unstructured debate among them.

featured.title: Improving Coherence and Persistence in Agentic AI for System Optimization
featured.authors: Pantea Karimi, Kimia Noorbakhsh, et al.
featured.gloss: Takes on the unglamorous half of composition: keeping a long-running agent coherent and on task as it works a real system across many steps.

movements.label: Measure
movements.headline: Before trusting the new tools, the field built the means to measure them, and pointed them at its hottest topic first.
movements.framing: Twelve papers, the second-largest group, are the field building its own rulers: benchmarks for vibe coding, tool use, persuasion, and domain agents, plus methods for catching agents in the act of failing. This is where the year’s most-discussed idea, vibe coding, gets held to an evaluation standard rather than taken on faith.

featured.title: ViBench: A Benchmark on Vibe Coding
featured.authors: Peter Zhong, Pashootan Vaezipoor, et al.
featured.affiliation: Replit, Georgian AI Lab, with Carnegie Mellon
featured.gloss: Builds a benchmark for vibe coding from production traces across fifteen applications, turning the year’s most-hyped practice into a measured, pass-or-fail task.

featured.title: Willful Disobedience: Automatically Detecting Failures in Agentic Traces
featured.authors: Reshabh K Sharma, Shraddha Barke, Benjamin Zorn
featured.affiliation: University of Washington and Microsoft Research
featured.gloss: A method for spotting where an agent went off the rails inside its own execution trace, so failures surface without a human reading every step.

featured.title: Reasoning-Intensive Regression
featured.gloss: Defines a class of prediction tasks that demand reasoning rather than pattern-matching, and shows where today’s models still break on them.

movements.label: Secure
movements.headline: The work the field recognized most was the work that makes agents fail safely.
movements.framing: Eleven papers took up security and privacy directly. It is not the largest group, but it holds the year’s highest recognition: two of the three Outstanding Paper awards sit here, alongside a third Outstanding Solution Paper, filed under architecture, that proves multi-agent coordination correct. Read together, they mark a field turning its attention from whether agents work to whether they can be trusted to.

featured.title: Malice in Agentland: Down the Rabbit Hole of Backdoors in the AI Supply Chain
featured.gloss: Shows how a poisoned tool or environment can plant a backdoor that lies dormant until a trigger appears in context, turning the agent supply chain itself into an attack surface.

featured.title: Securing Agents With Tracked Capabilities
featured.authors: Martin Odersky, Yaoyu Zhao, Yichen Xu, Oliver Bračevac, Cao Nguyen Pham
featured.gloss: Brings capability tracking to agents, so that what a tool is permitted to touch is checked and bounded by construction rather than trusted by default.

featured.title: TraceFix: Repairing Agent Coordination Protocols with TLA+ Counterexamples
featured.authors: Shuren Xia, Qiwei Li, Taqiya Ehsan, Jorge Ortiz
featured.gloss: Uses formal model checking to catch multi-agent coordination failures such as deadlock and resource races, then repairs the protocol from the counterexample.
